role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Incentives: who is paid for what
summary: People respond to how they are paid more reliably than to what they are asked to do. Every adviser and contractor you hire has a fee basis that pulls them in a direction, which is the principal-agent problem in practice. Draw the incentive map before you hire, and design fees so that their pull points where yours does.
body:
People do what they are paid to do more reliably than what they are asked to do. Before you hire anyone, draw the incentive map: how each party is paid, and what they gain or lose when the project goes well, badly or late. Then design the fee so that their pull points the same way as yours.

Recall

Q. In lesson 11, what can remove the protection a careful decision process would otherwise earn?

A. An undeclared conflict of interest.

Q. In lesson 1, why is the developer the person paid last?

A. Because every other party has a contract that pays them first; the developer receives only the residual.

Q. In lesson 8, what is a reference class?

A. A group of past projects similar enough to yours that their outcomes inform your forecast.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this week is about the psychology of deals, and incentives come first because they explain more behaviour than any personality trait. When an adviser recommends something, part of the recommendation is their judgment and part is their fee. You cannot see the split, so you must reason about it. A developer who understands incentives hires better, negotiates better and is surprised less. In lesson 6 you filled in an incentive table before a gate meeting. Today you learn to design incentives, not just read them.

The principal-agent problem

In plain English: when you hire someone to act for you, they are not you. They have their own interests, and they usually know more about their part of the work than you do. So you cannot check everything they do, and their interests and yours can quietly diverge.

The professional term is the principal-agent problem. The principal is the person whose interest is at stake, here you. The agent is the person acting on the principal's behalf: an architect, a broker, a project manager, a contractor, even a lawyer. The problem is not that agents are dishonest. Most are honest. The problem is that even an honest person, faced with many small judgment calls, will tend to resolve close calls in the direction their pay points.

There is good evidence for this in real estate itself. The economists Steven Levitt and Chad Syverson studied house sales and found that when real estate agents sold their own homes, they tended to keep them on the market longer and achieve higher prices than when they sold homes for clients. The plausible reading is not dishonesty. On a client's sale, the agent receives only a small share of any extra price but bears much of the extra effort and the risk of losing the sale, so waiting for a better offer is worth less to the agent than to the owner.

Fee basis: every fee pulls somewhere

The fee basis is the way a party's payment is calculated. Each basis pulls in a predictable direction.

Fee basisWhat it rewardsThe pull
Percentage of construction costHigher costToward upgrades and away from savings
Fixed lump sumLess effort for the same feeToward doing the minimum, and toward change orders
Hourly rateMore hoursToward process and away from speed
Commission on closingA closed dealToward speed and away from price discipline
Success fee on a targetHitting the targetToward the target, and toward gaming its definition

None of these is wrong. Each is a tool with a known pull. Which basis is common in your market for each discipline is commercial practice, not a standard, and it varies.

Worked example one. This is hypothetical. An architect is paid 6 percent of construction cost on a $10 million building, so $600,000. During design development, an upgrade to the facade is proposed that adds $1 million to construction cost. If you accept it, the architect's fee rises by $60,000, and the architect also gets a better-looking building for their portfolio. The upgrade may still be right. But notice that the person recommending it is paid more if you agree, and you are paid less. Your response is not suspicion; it is a question: "Price the upgrade, and tell me what it adds to rent or value."

Say that out loud now.

The incentive map

An incentive map is a simple table, drawn before you hire, listing each party and what happens to them in three outcomes: the project goes well, goes badly, or goes late. It shows you where interests diverge from yours, which tells you where to look hardest and what to renegotiate.

Worked example two, hypothetical. Your project manager is paid a monthly fee for the duration of construction. Map it: if the project goes well and finishes early, the project manager earns less, because there are fewer months. If it goes late, they earn more. That is an incentive pointing directly against your interest in time, the lever lesson 10 showed is worth about $23,000 a week on our hypothetical project.

Redesign it. Keep a monthly fee to cover their costs, but cap the total at the planned duration, and add a completion bonus paid if substantial completion is achieved by the reference-class date, with the bonus reduced for each week late. Now their pull points toward finishing, and they share the cost of delay. The amounts and terms are commercial choices for you and your lawyer to set. Professional sign-off required: lawyer, for the contract wording.

How the best do it

Some large public owners have gone furthest in aligning incentives through what is called alliance contracting, used notably on Australian infrastructure. In an alliance, the owner, designers and contractors agree a target cost and share the savings if the project comes in below it and the pain if it comes in above it, so that every party gains or loses together rather than at each other's expense. A small developer cannot replicate a full alliance, but can copy its core: tie part of each key adviser's pay to the outcome you care about, such as final cost, completion date or rent achieved, instead of to the volume of their own work.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is hiring an adviser whose fee rewards the opposite of your interest, without noticing, and then trusting their recommendations as if they were neutral. The control is to draw the incentive map before every engagement of any size, and either redesign the fee or apply extra scrutiny where the pull runs against you.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner makes one of two opposite mistakes. Either he assumes good people are immune to incentives, so he does not check; or he assumes anyone with a contrary incentive is dishonest, so he insults good advisers. Both miss the point. Incentives act on honest people at the margin, in the close calls. Design for that, and you can trust people and still be protected.

A practical habit makes the map cheap enough to use every time. Before any engagement, ask the adviser one plain question: "How are you paid if this goes well, if it goes badly, and if it goes late?" A good adviser answers easily and often volunteers where their pull runs against yours. Write the three answers in your file beside the fee proposal. Ten minutes of mapping on a hypothetical $600,000 design fee is the cheapest risk control you will buy on the project, and it changes the tone of the relationship: you are not accusing anyone, you are showing that you understand how work gets done.

Callback

In lesson 2, Ford pointed out that at Berlin, each package contractor was paid for its own package and nobody except the owner was paid for the whole building. That was an incentive map with a hole in it. When nobody is paid for the outcome you care about, nobody delivers it, and the incentive map is how you find the hole before you start.

Recap

Incentives shape behaviour at the margin, even among honest people. The principal-agent problem means your agents' interests and knowledge differ from yours. Every fee basis pulls somewhere: percentage fees toward cost, lump sums toward minimum effort, monthly fees toward delay, commissions toward closing. Draw the incentive map before you hire, then redesign fees so the pull points your way.

Next: Ford, Failure Forensics — Champlain Towers South, when the cost of acting is felt now and the risk is felt later.
checklist: Draw an incentive map before every engagement: how each party is paid and what they gain if the project goes well, badly or late.
Identify each adviser's fee basis and its pull.
When an adviser recommends an option that raises their fee, ask for the price and the effect on value.
Cap duration-based fees at the planned duration where you can.
Tie part of key advisers' pay to your outcome: cost, date or rent achieved.
Find the hole in the map: the outcome nobody is paid to deliver.
Have a lawyer draft any incentive terms.
head: Field checklist
speak: People do what they are paid to do more reliably than what they are asked to do. When I hire someone to act for me, that is the principal-agent problem: their interests and knowledge differ from mine, and even honest people resolve close calls in the direction of their pay. Every fee basis pulls somewhere. A percentage of construction cost rewards higher cost; on a hypothetical ten million dollar building, a million-dollar upgrade adds sixty thousand to a six percent fee. A monthly fee rewards delay. A commission rewards closing over price. So before I hire, I draw an incentive map: what each party gains if the project goes well, badly or late. Then I redesign the fee, for example capping a monthly fee at the planned duration and adding a bonus for finishing on the reference-class date. And I look for the hole: the outcome nobody is paid to deliver.
terms: Principal-agent problem — the divergence of interests and knowledge between a person and the agent they hire to act for them.
Fee basis — the way a party's payment is calculated, such as a percentage of cost, a lump sum, an hourly rate or a commission.
Incentive map — a table of each party and what they gain or lose if the project goes well, badly or late.

hostile.q: From a prospective project manager: you want to cap my monthly fee. Are you saying you do not trust me?
hostile.a: No. I am saying I want us paid the same way: both better off if we finish on time. The cap covers the planned duration, and the completion bonus means you earn more by finishing early than by running late. If the delay is caused by me, the contract will say so and you will not carry it.

title: Champlain Towers South: when the cost of acting is felt now and the risk later
summary: In 2018 an engineer's report found major structural damage at Champlain Towers South in Surfside, Florida; repairs were debated and deferred while the estimated cost rose, and a large assessment was approved in April 2021. On 24 June 2021 the building partially collapsed and 98 people died. The decision-level root cause was governance that let the people who had to pay set the timing of a life-safety repair.
body:
Ninety-eight people died when Champlain Towers South partially collapsed in 2021, three years after an engineer reported major structural damage. This lesson does not assign the technical cause; that belongs to the official investigators. It studies the decisions, because the decision pattern, a certain cost now against an uncertain risk later, is one every owner will face.

Recall

Q. In lesson 12, how do you work backward from value to the maximum base estimate?

A. Divide value by one plus the hurdle to get maximum all-in cost, then divide by one plus the reference-class uplift, then check forward.

Q. What was Rule 1?

A. No date, announcement or sunk cost moves me past a gate. Only the gate's written criteria do.

Q. What was Rule 2?

A. Before I commit to a cost or a date, I write the reference-class figure beside my own estimate and explain any gap in writing.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, you will own buildings, and some of them will age. One day an engineer will hand you a report that says something expensive must be done, and you will be the one deciding when. This case is about that moment. It involves real people who died, and we study it with respect, to learn what should happen in the room when such a report arrives. Ford leads; Roman joins on the question of reserves.

Step 1: Timeline

Champlain Towers South was a 12-storey condominium building in Surfside, Florida, completed in 1981. As it approached its 40-year recertification, an engineering firm inspected it, and its October 2018 report described major structural damage to the concrete slab below the pool deck and entrance area, which it linked to failed waterproofing, as well as cracking and deterioration in the garage. It recommended repairs. Over the following years, the condominium association debated the scope, cost and funding of the work; there was disagreement on the board, and board members resigned. The estimated cost of the work grew. In April 2021, the association approved a large special assessment, reported at about $15 million, and the board's president wrote to owners that the concrete deterioration was accelerating. Major work had not been completed when, in the early hours of 24 June 2021, part of the building collapsed. Ninety-eight people died. A federal technical investigation was opened into the cause; check its current status and findings before drawing any technical conclusion.

Step 2: Key decisions

  • Treating the 2018 report's repairs as a project to be scoped, debated and funded over years, rather than as a safety matter to be acted on promptly.
  • Funding the work through a large, late special assessment rather than from reserves accumulated over time.
  • Allowing reassurance and disagreement to stand in for an engineer-led timeline.

Step 3: Assumptions

The key assumption was that the damage could wait: that a building which had stood for decades would stand for a few more years while the money was found. Underneath it sat a second assumption, that an engineer's report describes a repair list rather than a risk with a clock attached.

Step 4: Incentives

This is the heart of the case. A condominium association is usually governed by volunteer owners elected by other owners. The cost of acting was concentrated, certain and immediate: a special assessment, meaning a one-time charge levied on owners to fund work the regular budget cannot cover, running to tens of thousands of dollars per unit. The benefit of acting was diffuse, uncertain and invisible: a risk reduced, which looks like nothing happening.

Research on decision-making explains why that combination is so dangerous. Loss aversion, documented by Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky, is the tendency for a loss to feel roughly twice as painful as an equal gain feels good. A certain, visible loss today, the assessment, looms far larger than a probable, invisible loss later. Board members also faced their neighbours every day; those who pushed for the full cost bore the social price. Every incentive in the room pointed toward later.

Say that out loud now.

Step 5: Warning signs ignored

The report itself used the language of major damage. The cost estimate rose over time, which is what deterioration looks like on a spreadsheet. Board members resigned amid disagreement, a sign that the governance process could not resolve the decision. And by April 2021 the association's own leadership described the deterioration as accelerating. Each was a signal that the timeline was being set by the funding debate rather than by the building.

Step 6: Point of no return

The physical point of no return is a technical question for the investigators, and this lesson does not answer it. The decision-level lesson is clearer: the period in which the problem was a repair project rather than an emergency was spent on debate about scope and money. When the people paying for a safety repair also control its timing, delay is the default outcome, and each month of delay shortens a margin nobody can measure from a meeting room.

Step 7: Root cause

At the level of decisions, the root cause was governance that let the people who had to pay set the timing of a life-safety repair, without reserves to soften the cost, and with reassurance accepted in place of an engineer-led schedule. Florida later changed its law on condominium safety inspections and reserves; verify the current requirements against the primary source before relying on them.

Applied examples at your scale

This is a composite example. A developer owns a 20-year-old rental building. A facade engineer reports that balcony slab edges show corrosion of reinforcement and recommends repairs within twelve months, with interim measures now. The developer's cash is committed to a new project. The temptation is to put up a notice, restrict a few balconies and wait for next year's budget. Rule 3 says the engineer's timeline sets the date: fund the interim measures now, schedule the repairs inside the twelve months, and if the cash is not there, the new project waits. Professional sign-off required: structural engineer.

A second composite, about reserves. A developer selling condominium units sets the initial monthly fees low to help sales, with a thin reserve fund, the money an owners' association sets aside for future major repairs and replacements. Low fees help sell units today; a thin reserve hands the next generation of owners a special assessment, and the loss-aversion trap described above. A responsible developer funds reserves from a professional reserve study rather than from the sales pitch, and the applicable law may set minimums; verify against the primary source.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is letting the funding debate set the safety timeline. The control is Rule 3, written into your own governance: when a qualified engineer reports a structural or life-safety defect, the engineer's recommended timeline is the schedule, interim measures are taken immediately, and funding is found to fit it.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner hears reassurance and relaxes. He asks a second person until someone says it can wait. The professional notices when he is shopping for the answer he wants, and goes back to the qualified engineer with one question: "What is the latest date by which this must be done, and what must we do in the meantime?"

Callback

In lesson 6, Remi warned that a strong voice in the room can replace the criteria with a story. Here the story was reassurance, and the criteria should have been the engineer's report. In lesson 10, Priya showed that delay compounds; on a deteriorating structure it compounds physically as well as financially.

Recap

An engineer reported major structural damage in 2018; repairs were debated and deferred while costs rose; a large assessment came in April 2021; on 24 June 2021 the building partially collapsed and 98 people died. The technical cause belongs to the investigators. The decision lesson is that a certain cost today is felt more than an uncertain risk tomorrow. Rule 3: when a qualified engineer reports a structural or life-safety defect, I fund and schedule the fix on the engineer's timeline. Cost, reassurance and the wish to wait never set the date.

Next: JAX, The Money — anchors: the first number on the table and your walk-away price.
checklist: Treat every structural or life-safety finding as a risk with a clock, not a repair list.
Ask the engineer for the latest safe completion date and the interim measures required now.
Take interim measures immediately, before funding is settled.
Separate who sets the safety timeline from who pays for the work.
Fund reserves from a professional reserve study, not from the sales pitch.
Notice when you are shopping for reassurance, and stop.
Verify the current legal requirements on inspections and reserves against the primary source.
head: Field checklist
speak: Champlain Towers South, a 12-storey condominium in Surfside, Florida, was inspected ahead of its 40-year recertification, and a 2018 engineer's report described major structural damage below the pool deck. The repairs were debated and deferred while the estimated cost rose, board members resigned, and a large special assessment was approved only in April 2021, with the board warning that deterioration was accelerating. On 24 June 2021 part of the building collapsed and 98 people died. The technical cause belongs to the investigators. The decision lesson is about incentives and loss aversion: a certain, visible cost today feels larger than an uncertain risk tomorrow, and the owners who had to pay also controlled the timing. My rule: when a qualified engineer reports a structural or life-safety defect, I fund and schedule the fix on the engineer's timeline. Cost, reassurance and the wish to wait never set the date.
terms: Loss aversion — the tendency, documented by Kahneman and Tversky, for a loss to feel roughly twice as painful as an equal gain feels good.
Special assessment — a one-time charge levied on owners in an association to fund work the regular budget cannot cover.
Reserve fund — money an owners' association sets aside over time for future major repairs and replacements.

hostile.q: From your lender: the facade report says repairs within twelve months. Your cash is committed to the new project. Which comes first?
hostile.a: The repairs. Interim measures are already in place, the repair contract will be signed inside the engineer's timeline, and if that means the new project's equity is delayed, the new project waits. I will send you the engineer's letter and the repair schedule this week.

rule: Rule 3: When a qualified engineer reports a structural or life-safety defect, I fund and schedule the fix on the engineer's timeline. Cost, reassurance and the wish to wait never set the date.

title: Anchors: the first number on the table and your walk-away price
summary: The first number in a negotiation pulls every later number toward it, even when it is arbitrary. The defence is to calculate your own number first: the residual land value, the most you can pay for land and still earn your required profit. That figure becomes your walk-away price, set before you hear the seller's.
body:
The first number on the table pulls every later number toward it, even when you know it is arbitrary. The defence is to calculate your own number before you hear theirs: the residual land value, the most the land can cost while the project still earns your required profit. That is your walk-away price.

Recall

Q. In lesson 13, why should everyone write alone before speaking in a pre-mortem?

A. Because once the leader speaks, everyone else's list shrinks to match it.

Q. In lesson 3, what is profit on cost?

A. Development profit divided by total development cost.

Q. In lesson 10, why does delay hurt IRR more than profit?

A. Because it reduces profit through carry and pushes the return later, and time is in the denominator of an annual return.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, land is usually the first large commitment in a project and the one you can least easily undo. Overpay for it and the profit is gone before the first drawing, because every other cost still has to be paid in full. Land prices are also where anchoring does its most expensive work, because the seller's asking price arrives first and sounds like information. It usually is not.

Anchoring

In plain English: anchoring is the tendency for any number you hear first to drag your estimate toward it. The psychologists Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman demonstrated it with a wheel of fortune rigged to stop at either a high or a low number. People who saw the higher number then gave higher estimates of an unrelated quantity than people who saw the lower one, even though they knew the wheel was random. Later research has found anchoring effects among experienced professionals too, including in property valuation.

The professional framing: in a negotiation, the first credible number sets the range in which the rest of the conversation happens. An asking price of $3 million makes $2.7 million feel like a good deal, whether or not the land is worth $2.7 million to you. The anchor does not have to be believed to work; it only has to be heard.

Your own anchor: residual land value

Residual land value is the most you can pay for the land and still earn your required profit. You calculate it by starting from the completed value, subtracting every cost other than land, and subtracting the profit you require. What is left is what the land can bear. It is the same reverse logic Quincy taught in lesson 12, pointed at the land.

Worked example one. This is hypothetical. The completed building is worth $16,000,000. Every cost other than land, including construction, fees, finance and contingency at your chosen percentile, comes to $11,500,000. You require 15 percent profit on total cost, a commercial choice, not a standard.

  1. Maximum total cost at a 15 percent profit on cost: $16,000,000 divided by 1.15 equals $13,913,000.
  2. Subtract the non-land costs: $13,913,000 minus $11,500,000 equals $2,413,000.
  3. That is the residual land value: about $2.41 million, including your purchase costs such as legal fees and any transfer taxes.

Your walk-away price, the price above which you will not buy, is $2.41 million, all in. You write it down and sign it before you meet the seller.

Say that out loud now.

What the anchor costs you

Worked example two. The seller's broker opens at $3,000,000, citing a sale down the street. You negotiate hard and feel good when you get to $2,700,000. But measure it against your own number.

  • At $2,700,000, total cost is $11,500,000 plus $2,700,000, which is $14,200,000. Profit is $16,000,000 minus $14,200,000, which is $1,800,000. Profit on cost is about 12.7 percent, below your hurdle.
  • At the full $3,000,000, total cost is $14,500,000. Profit is $1,500,000, about 10.3 percent on cost.

The negotiation felt like a win because it was measured against the seller's anchor. Measured against yours, you have paid $287,000 more than the land can bear. That is money taken directly out of your residual, before a shovel enters the ground.

Handling the anchor in the room

Three practices help. First, calculate and sign your walk-away price before you hear any asking price, so that your anchor exists before theirs. Second, when you hear their number, do not respond to it directly. Respond with your own reasoning: "Based on what the finished building can carry, land works for us at around $2.3 million." That sets a counter-anchor grounded in arithmetic rather than in their number. Third, examine their justification. A sale down the street may have had different zoning, a different size, or a buyer with a different plan. Ask what it was, and adjust.

There is also an anchor inside your own office. Once you have built a pro forma at the asking price, that model becomes an anchor too, and every revision feels like a loss from it. Build your first model from the residual, never from the asking price.

Why the land absorbs every error

Residual land value is sensitive, because land is what is left over. Every mistake in value or cost lands on it in full, while being only a small share of the total. That is a kind of leverage, and it runs both ways.

Worked example three, hypothetical, using the same project. Suppose your completed value is 3 percent too optimistic, and the building is really worth $15,500,000 rather than $16,000,000.

  1. Maximum total cost: $15,500,000 divided by 1.15 equals about $13,478,000.
  2. Subtract the non-land costs of $11,500,000: the residual is about $1,978,000.
  3. The residual has fallen by about $435,000, roughly 18 percent, from a 3 percent change in value.

Now leave value at $16,000,000 and let non-land costs run 5 percent over, to $12,075,000. The residual becomes $13,913,000 minus $12,075,000, which is about $1,838,000, a fall of $575,000, roughly 24 percent. Small errors in the big numbers become large errors in the small one. So your walk-away price is only as good as the value and cost evidence underneath it, and you should run it at your cautious value and your P80 cost before you sign it, not only at your base case. If the deal works only at your most hopeful inputs, the honest walk-away price is lower than the base case says.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is winning the negotiation and losing the deal: paying less than asked but more than the residual. The control is a signed walk-away price, calculated from your own pro forma before you meet the seller, and a rule that any increase requires the pro forma to be changed with evidence, not just the price.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner raises his walk-away price in the room because the seller seemed reasonable, the site is lovely, and he has already spent weeks on it. That is anchoring, liking and sunk cost working together. The professional changes the walk-away price only when an input to the residual calculation changes, such as better evidence of rent, and then shows the change on paper.

There is an opposite error, and it is worth naming. A counter-anchor set absurdly low, with no reasoning behind it, can end the conversation or mark you as unserious. The strength of your number comes from the arithmetic you can show, not from how far it sits below theirs. Offer the number with its reasons, and be ready to walk the seller through them.

Callback

In lesson 5, Roman showed that the most a study is worth is the expected loss it avoids, and in lesson 12, Quincy worked backward from a required margin. The residual land value is the same reverse method applied to the most important price you will pay. Every one of these tools exists to put your number on the table before someone else's.

Recap

Anchoring pulls every later number toward the first one, even when it is arbitrary. Your defence is your own anchor: the residual land value, which is completed value minus all non-land costs minus your required profit. In the example it is about $2.41 million, and paying $2.7 million after a hard negotiation still overpays by $287,000. Set and sign your walk-away price before you hear theirs, and change it only when the inputs change.

Next: LEX, The Rules — what the law says about persuasion: puffery, misrepresentation and the entire-agreement clause.
checklist: Calculate the residual land value before you hear any asking price.
Include purchase costs such as legal fees and transfer taxes in the land figure.
Write and sign your walk-away price before the first meeting.
Respond to an asking price with your own reasoning, not with a counter-number pegged to theirs.
Examine every comparable sale the seller cites: zoning, size, timing, buyer.
Build your first pro forma from the residual, never from the asking price.
Change the walk-away price only when an input changes, and show the change on paper.
head: Field checklist
speak: The first number in a negotiation pulls everything toward it, even when I know it is arbitrary. That is anchoring. My defence is to set my own anchor first: the residual land value, which is the completed value minus every non-land cost minus the profit I require. On a hypothetical building worth sixteen million, with eleven and a half million of non-land costs and a fifteen percent profit on cost, the land can bear about 2.41 million, all in. That is my walk-away price, signed before I meet the seller. If the broker opens at three million and I negotiate down to 2.7, it feels like a win, but I have paid about 287 thousand more than the land can carry, and my profit on cost falls to about 12.7 percent. So I answer their number with my reasoning, I examine their comparables, and I change my walk-away price only when an input changes.
terms: Anchoring — the tendency for the first number you hear to pull your later estimates toward it.
Residual land value — the most you can pay for land: completed value minus all non-land costs minus your required profit.
Walk-away price — the price above which you will not buy, set and written down before negotiating.

hostile.q: From the seller's broker: the lot down the street sold for three million last spring. Why should my client take two point three?
hostile.a: Because that is what the finished building can carry at the return our lender and investors require; I will walk you through the residual. If that sale had different zoning or a buyer with a different plan, it does not change our arithmetic. If your client has evidence that changes an input, I will look at it.

title: What the law says about persuasion: puffery, misrepresentation and the entire-agreement clause
summary: Persuasion is legal; false statements of fact that induce a contract can be actionable as misrepresentation, while vague sales talk generally is not. An entire-agreement clause may limit what pre-contract statements you can rely on. So verify every fact that matters, put the ones you rely on into the contract, and hold yourself to the same standard when you are the one persuading.
body:
The law generally lets people persuade, praise and exaggerate in vague terms. It is far less forgiving of false statements of fact that lead someone into a contract. The practical rule runs both ways: verify every fact you rely on and get it into the contract, and never state a fact you have not checked when you are the one persuading.

Recall

Q. In lesson 14's Red Pen, what was wrong with "the general contractor is a company in which my business partner has an interest"?

A. It was an undeclared conflict of interest that should have been declared and handled before the decision.

Q. In lesson 4, what is an adopted code?

A. The specific edition of a model code, with local amendments, that a jurisdiction has made law.

Q. In lesson 11, what makes a decision defensible under the business judgment idea?

A. Being informed, in good faith, unconflicted, reasonable and recorded; the precise test varies and must be verified.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this week is about how people are influenced in deals. Influence techniques are mostly legal. What the law cares about is whether a statement of fact was true, whether it mattered, and whether the other side relied on it. You will be on both sides: hearing claims from sellers and brokers, and making claims to lenders, investors and buyers. This lesson teaches the general concepts, drawn mainly from common-law traditions. Whether and how they apply depends on the jurisdiction and the facts, so verify against the primary source and take legal advice before relying on them. Professional sign-off required: real estate lawyer.

Puffery, opinion and fact

In plain English: some statements are just sales talk, and the law generally expects you to discount them. Others are claims about facts you can check, and those are the ones that matter legally.

Puffery is vague, exaggerated praise that no reasonable person would take as a verifiable fact: "the best location in the city", "a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity". Courts in many systems treat puffery as not actionable. An honest opinion is also generally treated differently from a fact, though an opinion from someone with special knowledge, or one that implies facts that are untrue, can cross the line. A statement of fact is a claim that can be checked: "the site is zoned for 40 units", "the building next door leases at $2,000 a month".

Worked example one. A seller's broker says three things about a hypothetical site.

  • "This is the best block in the neighbourhood." Puffery. Ignore it.
  • "In my view, rents here will keep rising." Opinion. Weigh it against the broker's incentive to close, which you mapped in lesson 15.
  • "The site is zoned for 40 units." A statement of fact. It is exactly the kind of claim to verify with the authority having jurisdiction and, if you rely on it, to put into the contract as a representation.

Misrepresentation

In common-law traditions, a misrepresentation is, broadly, a false statement of fact made by one party to another which induces that other party to enter a contract. Depending on the system and on whether the statement was made fraudulently, carelessly or innocently, the remedies can include undoing the contract, called rescission, and damages. The categories, the tests and the remedies differ between jurisdictions and are subject to statute; verify them against the primary source.

The practical points hold widely. A misrepresentation claim usually requires a false statement of fact, that it was material, and that you actually relied on it. Each of those can be fought over. And fighting over them is slow and expensive. The law is a remedy after the damage, not a substitute for checking.

Say that out loud now.

The entire-agreement clause

Many commercial contracts include an entire-agreement clause, which states that the written contract is the whole agreement between the parties and replaces anything said or written before it. Some go further, with a non-reliance clause, in which each party states that it did not rely on any statement not written into the contract. The purpose is certainty: the deal is what is on the page.

The effect on you is direct. If a broker told you the site was zoned for 40 units, and the contract contains such clauses but no representation about zoning, you may find it much harder to rely on what you were told. How far these clauses are enforced, and whether they can exclude liability for fraud or for certain misrepresentations, varies by jurisdiction and may be limited by statute; verify against the primary source.

Worked example two, a composite. A developer buys a site after the seller's agent tells him the soil has been tested and is suitable for conventional foundations. The purchase agreement has an entire-agreement clause and no representation about soil. After closing, the developer's own investigation finds poor soil requiring deep foundations. His lawyer explains that recovering the extra cost may be difficult, slow and uncertain. The fix would have cost almost nothing before signing: either commission his own soil report as a condition of the purchase, or require the seller to provide the existing report and represent in the contract that it is the complete and accurate report in the seller's possession.

When you are the one persuading

The same law applies to you. When you tell a lender your costs are fixed, tell an investor the zoning is approved, or tell a condominium buyer the building will be finished by a date, you are making statements that may be relied on. Investment and consumer statements may also be governed by securities and consumer protection laws with stricter rules, which later weeks cover. The discipline is simple: state facts you have verified, say "we expect" or "our estimate is" when you mean a forecast, and keep the evidence.

Turning the reliance list into contract terms

Worked example three, hypothetical. Before signing for a site, a developer writes down four facts he is relying on, and decides what to do with each.

Fact relied onVerify itOr put it in the contract
The site is zoned for 40 unitsWritten confirmation from the authority having jurisdictionA condition that the purchase completes only if the zoning is confirmed
There are no tenants or occupiersA site visit and a title searchA representation that vacant possession will be given on closing
The existing soil report is completeHis own geotechnical investigationA representation that the report provided is the complete report in the seller's possession
No environmental notices have been issuedAn environmental site assessment by his own consultantA representation, and a condition tied to the assessment

Each row is either checked or contracted, and the most important are both. The cost is a few weeks of conditions and some consultant fees. The cost of skipping it is the composite soil case above, repeated for whichever fact turns out to be wrong. Which representations a seller will give, and how long they survive after closing, are negotiated terms, not standards. Professional sign-off required: real estate lawyer and geotechnical engineer.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is relying on something you were told and signing a contract that does not contain it. The control is a reliance list: before signing, write down every fact you are relying on, then confirm that each one is either independently verified or written into the contract as a representation or a condition, with your lawyer's advice on the wording.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner assumes that if he was misled, the law will fix it. Sometimes it will, years later, at great cost, if he can prove reliance and materiality and get past the clauses he signed. The professional assumes the opposite: anything not verified or not in the contract is not there.

Callback

In lesson 6, Remi gave you the line "Is that in writing?" for the gate meeting. This lesson tells you why it matters legally as well as practically. A fact that lives only in a conversation may, after signing, be a fact you cannot use.

Recap

Puffery is vague praise and generally not actionable; opinion is weighed by its source; statements of fact are what matter. A misrepresentation is, broadly, a false statement of fact that induces a contract, with remedies that vary by jurisdiction. Entire-agreement and non-reliance clauses can limit what you may rely on. Keep a reliance list, verify or contract every item, and hold your own statements to the same standard.

Next: Sage, The Numbers — sunk cost arithmetic: deciding from today forward.
checklist: Sort every claim you hear into puffery, opinion or statement of fact.
Verify every statement of fact that affects value with the primary source or authority.
Keep a reliance list of every fact you are relying on before signing.
Put each relied-on fact into the contract as a representation or condition, or verify it independently.
Read the entire-agreement and non-reliance clauses before signing, with your lawyer.
Say “we expect” or “our estimate is” when you mean a forecast.
Keep the evidence behind every fact you state to lenders, investors and buyers.
head: Field checklist
speak: The law generally lets people persuade and praise. Vague sales talk like best location in the city is puffery, and it is usually not actionable. Opinions are weighed by their source. What matters is a statement of fact, like the site is zoned for forty units. In common-law traditions, a false statement of fact that induces a contract can be a misrepresentation, with remedies that may include undoing the contract or damages, though the tests vary by jurisdiction. But many contracts contain an entire-agreement clause saying the written document is the whole deal, and sometimes a non-reliance clause too, which can make it hard to rely on anything you were only told. So before I sign, I keep a reliance list: every fact I am relying on is either verified independently or written into the contract. And I hold my own statements to lenders, investors and buyers to the same standard.
terms: Puffery — vague, exaggerated sales praise that no reasonable person would treat as a verifiable fact.
Misrepresentation — broadly, a false statement of fact by one party that induces another to enter a contract.
Entire-agreement clause — a contract term stating that the written contract is the whole agreement and replaces prior statements.

hostile.q: From the seller's lawyer: our client will not give a representation on zoning. Your client can do his own diligence. Will he proceed?
hostile.a: He will proceed only with a condition: the purchase is conditional on our own written confirmation of zoning from the authority within a set period, with the deposit returnable if it is not obtained. If your client is confident in the zoning, that condition costs him nothing.

title: Sunk cost arithmetic: deciding from today forward
summary: Money already spent appears in every option, so it cannot change which option is best; only future costs and future receipts can. Loss aversion makes selling at a loss feel worse than it is, so the professional compares options from today forward, adds the reference-class view of future costs, and counts the opportunity cost of the capital.
body:
Money already spent is gone whichever option you choose, so it cannot change which option is best. Only what you will spend and receive from today forward can. Loss aversion makes walking away at a loss feel worse than it is, so you run the numbers forward, with the outside view, and count what the money could do elsewhere.

Recall

Q. In lesson 15, what is the principal-agent problem?

A. The divergence of interests and knowledge between a person and the agent they hire to act for them.

Q. In lesson 5, what two checks come before accepting a positive expected value?

A. That the expected value is positive, and that the worst plausible outcome is survivable.

Q. In lesson 12, what does P80 mean?

A. The outcome that 80 percent of comparable projects did better than; a bad-but-not-unusual case.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, at some point you will own a project that has gone sideways: costs up, value flat, money already in. The question will be whether to keep going or get out. Rule 1 already says sunk cost cannot move you past a gate. This lesson gives you the arithmetic, so that the decision is made on numbers rather than on the pain of admitting a loss.

Three terms

A sunk cost is money already spent that cannot be recovered whatever you decide. Opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative use of the same money or time; capital tied up in one project is capital not earning elsewhere. A forward-looking comparison sets options side by side using only future costs and future receipts from today, ignoring sunk costs because they are common to every option.

Worked example one: the sunk cost cancels

This is hypothetical. You bought a site for $2,500,000 and have spent $600,000 on design and approvals, so $3,100,000 is sunk. A new estimate puts the remaining cost to build at $11,800,000. The completed building is worth $15,500,000. A buyer offers $2,600,000 for the site with its approvals, net of selling costs.

Total view, including sunk costs:

  • Build: $15,500,000 minus ($3,100,000 plus $11,800,000) equals a profit of $600,000.
  • Sell: $2,600,000 minus $3,100,000 equals a loss of $500,000.
  • Difference: building is better by $1,100,000.

Forward view, from today:

  • Build: receive $15,500,000, spend $11,800,000: a forward gain of $3,700,000.
  • Sell: receive $2,600,000, spend nothing: a forward gain of $2,600,000.
  • Difference: building is better by $1,100,000.

The answer is identical. The $3,100,000 appears in both options in the total view and subtracts out. That is the whole argument against sunk-cost reasoning: what you have spent cannot tell you which option is better, because it is the same in every option.

Say that out loud now.

Where the psychology bites

If the arithmetic is that simple, why do people get it wrong? Because of how the options feel. Selling "locks in a loss of $500,000". Building "might still make $600,000". Loss aversion, which Ford introduced in lesson 16, makes the certain loss feel roughly twice as bad as an equal gain feels good, so the uncertain path to a profit feels much more attractive than it should. The forward view removes the word "loss" from the comparison, which is exactly why it helps.

But notice that the example above used your own estimate of $11,800,000. Rule 2 says to put the reference class beside it.

Worked example two: forward, with the outside view

Suppose your reference class shows remaining-cost overruns of 8 percent at P50 and 18 percent at P80.

  • At P50, remaining cost is $11,800,000 times 1.08, which equals $12,744,000. Forward gain from building: $15,500,000 minus $12,744,000, which is $2,756,000. Selling gives $2,600,000. Building is better by only $156,000.
  • At P80, remaining cost is $11,800,000 times 1.18, which equals $13,924,000. Forward gain from building: $1,576,000. Selling is better by $1,024,000.

Now the decision looks completely different. Building commits about $12 million or more of new money, takes perhaps 18 months more of carry and risk, and on a typical outcome beats a certain $2.6 million by only $156,000. In a bad-but-not-unusual outcome, it loses by about $1 million.

Then add the opportunity cost. The $2,600,000 received from a sale is free to fund another project, or to sit as liquidity, while the build option ties up your equity for the duration. If that freed capital could reasonably earn even a modest return over 18 months, the case for building weakens further.

This lesson does not say you must sell. A developer with evidence of higher rents, a cheaper contractor price or a strong balance sheet might reasonably build. It says the decision must be made between $2.6 million certain today and a forward gain that is thin at P50 and negative at P80, not between "losing half a million" and "making six hundred thousand". The second framing is the one loss aversion writes for you.

Worked example three: what is really sunk, and the value of time

Not everything already signed is sunk. Some past decisions create future cash flows, and those belong in the forward view. Read your contracts before you compare.

Suppose the design contract says that if you stop the project, you owe the architect a termination fee of $150,000. That fee is not sunk; it is a future cost of the sell option only. The forward gain from selling becomes $2,600,000 minus $150,000, which is $2,450,000. At P50, building now beats selling by $2,756,000 minus $2,450,000, which is $306,000. A deposit you could still recover would work the other way, as a future receipt in whichever option returns it.

Now add the timing. The sale money arrives today; the build gain arrives in about 18 months. Suppose, hypothetically, that freed capital could earn 6 percent a year in a simple, low-risk use. $2,600,000 for 18 months at 6 percent earns $2,600,000 times 0.06 times 1.5, which is $234,000, so the sale is worth about $2,834,000 by the time the building would be finished. Against the P50 build gain of $2,756,000, ignoring the termination fee, selling is now better by about $78,000. The 6 percent is a placeholder for your own cost of capital, not a recommendation; use the rate you would actually earn or pay. The point is method: forward cash flows only, at the same date, with the outside view applied.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is throwing good money after bad to avoid recognising a loss. The control is a rule for every reset gate: present the options only in the forward view, with the reference class applied to future costs and the opportunity cost of the capital stated, and remove sunk costs from the decision page entirely. Keep them in the accounts, where they belong.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner says, "We cannot sell now; we have too much in it." The amount in it is exactly what does not matter. A useful test: imagine you did not own the site, and someone offered it to you with its approvals for $2.6 million. Would you buy it and build? If not, you should probably not keep it and build either.

One more habit helps at a reset gate. Ask someone who did not make the original decision to build the forward comparison. The person who chose the site is the one most anchored to the money already in it, through no fault of character. A fresh analyst, given only today's numbers, has nothing to defend.

Callback

In lesson 7, Kema's Red Pen memo said, "We have already spent $180,000, so stopping now would waste that investment." Rule 1 rejected it as sunk cost. This lesson shows the arithmetic behind the rule: the $180,000 is in every option, so it can never decide between them.

Recap

Sunk costs appear in every option and cancel, so they cannot change the best choice. Compare options forward, from today: future receipts minus future costs. Apply the reference class to future costs, and count the opportunity cost of capital tied up. In the example, a $600,000 "profit" versus a $500,000 "loss" became $156,000 better at P50 and $1 million worse at P80. Remove sunk costs from the decision page.

Next: Kema, The Room — the influence room: Cialdini's principles across the table, and trust.
checklist: Remove sunk costs from the decision page; keep them in the accounts.
Compare every option in the forward view: future receipts minus future costs.
Apply the reference-class uplift to future costs, at P50 and P80.
State the opportunity cost of the capital each option ties up.
Ask: if I did not own this, would I buy it today at this price and proceed?
Watch for the words “lock in a loss”; they are loss aversion speaking.
Record the forward comparison in the gate note.
head: Field checklist
speak: Money already spent is in every option, so it cannot decide between them. On a hypothetical site with 3.1 million sunk, building shows a six hundred thousand profit and selling for 2.6 million shows a five hundred thousand loss. In the forward view, building gains 3.7 million against 2.6 for selling. Either way building is ahead by 1.1 million, because the sunk cost cancels. But that used my own estimate. Applying the reference class to the 11.8 million still to spend, at P50 building is ahead by only 156 thousand, and at P80 selling is ahead by about a million. Add the opportunity cost of tying up my equity for another year and a half. Loss aversion wants to avoid locking in a loss; the forward view removes that word. My test: if I did not own this site, would I buy it today and build? If not, I probably should not keep it and build.
terms: Sunk cost — money already spent that cannot be recovered whatever you decide.
Opportunity cost — the value of the best alternative use of the same money or time.
Forward-looking comparison — comparing options using only future costs and receipts from today.

hostile.q: From your investor: you are proposing to sell the site for less than we put in. Why should we accept a loss?
hostile.a: Because the money already spent is gone in both options; the real choice is $2.6 million now versus building, which on our reference class is only about $156,000 better on a typical outcome and about $1 million worse on a bad one, with more of your capital at risk for another eighteen months. I will show you both cases side by side.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: The influence room: Cialdini's principles across the table, and trust
summary: Robert Cialdini identified a small set of principles through which people are persuaded, including reciprocity, commitment and consistency, social proof, authority, liking and scarcity. In a land negotiation you will meet several in an hour. Name them silently, return to your written numbers, and build trust of your own through reliability rather than charm.
body:
The people across the table are trying to influence you, and most of them are doing nothing wrong. Learn the principles they use, name each one silently when it appears, and return to your written numbers. Then build your own trust the slow way: by being reliable.

Recall

Q. What was Rule 3?

A. When a qualified engineer reports a structural or life-safety defect, I fund and schedule the fix on the engineer's timeline. Cost, reassurance and the wish to wait never set the date.

Q. In lesson 6, what is the question behind a broker's "Can we firm up by Friday?"

A. Usually the commission, which is paid only at closing.

Q. In lesson 13, what should you say when someone brings bad news in a pre-mortem?

A. "Thank you. That is exactly the kind of thing I need to hear."

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, you will negotiate for land, loans, contracts and partners. In each room, someone will use the same handful of influence principles, often skilfully and often without thinking about it. You are not trying to become immune to persuasion; that is impossible and would make you a poor partner. You are trying to notice it, so that your decisions come from your numbers rather than from the atmosphere.

The principles

The psychologist Robert Cialdini, in his book Influence, described six principles through which people are reliably persuaded, and later added a seventh, unity, the pull of shared identity. In plain English:

  • Reciprocity. We feel obliged to return favours, even small, unrequested ones.
  • Commitment and consistency. Once we have said yes to something small, or stated a position, we feel pressure to act consistently with it.
  • Social proof. We look to what others are doing, especially people like us, to decide what is right.
  • Authority. We defer to people who appear to be experts.
  • Liking. We say yes more easily to people we like and who are like us.
  • Scarcity. We value things more when they seem rare or about to disappear.

The scene

This is a composite example. You meet a seller's broker for lunch to discuss a hypothetical site. You have already signed your walk-away price of $2.41 million, from lesson 17's residual calculation.

The broker insists on paying for lunch, and mentions he brought this site to you before anyone else. That is reciprocity. He asks, "You would agree this is one of the best locations in the area?" You nod. Twenty minutes later he says, "Since we agree it is a top location, a top price makes sense." That is commitment and consistency built on a small yes. He mentions that two well-known developers have bought nearby. Social proof. He says the city's planning director told him the area is "earmarked for growth". Authority, at second hand. He grew up near where you did and you have a lot in common. Liking. Finally: "There are two other parties, and the seller wants an answer by Friday." Scarcity.

None of it changes the residual. All of it is designed, consciously or not, to make $2.7 million feel reasonable.

Say that out loud now.

Lines to say, and lines never to say

  • When you hear a small agreement being collected, say: "It is a good location. What the land is worth to us depends on what the building can carry."
  • On the planning director: "Is that in writing? I will confirm it with the planning department directly."
  • On the deadline: "If the seller needs an answer by Friday, my answer by Friday is our number. If they want more time to consider it, so do we."
  • Never say: "I really want this site." It tells the other side your walk-away price is soft.
  • Never say: "What would it take to get this done today?" It hands the anchor back to them.

The question behind the question, and when to stay silent

When the broker asks, "What is your budget for land?", the question behind it is where your ceiling is, so he can price to it. Answer with your reasoning, not your ceiling. When he names a number after your counter, stay silent and let it sit. The silence often brings a concession, or information about the other parties, which may turn out to be less than was implied. If you feel the urge to fill the pause, write something down instead.

Trust: the part that is yours to build

Influence is about the other side moving you. Trust is about whether people will deal with you repeatedly, on good terms, over a career. David Maister and his co-authors, in The Trusted Advisor, proposed a trust equation: trustworthiness rises with credibility, reliability and intimacy, the sense that it is safe to share things with you, and falls with self-orientation, the sense that you are focused on yourself rather than on them. It is a practitioner's model, not a measured law, but it is a useful checklist.

For a developer, reliability is the cheapest and strongest of the four. Send the document when you said you would. Give your answer by the time you promised. Tell people bad news early. Brokers, lenders and contractors remember which developers do what they say, and the best deals often reach those developers first. That is how you earn the honest version of the reciprocity the broker was using on you.

Holding your state

Pleasant pressure is harder to resist than hostile pressure, because nothing triggers your guard. Watch for the physical sign of being moved: a warm sense of wanting the deal and wanting the other person to like you. When you feel it, slow down, take out your written numbers, and look at them before you speak. If the meal ends with a deadline, you can always say, "I will call you tomorrow by noon," and then do exactly that.

Unity, and the same principles in your hands

The seventh principle, unity, is the pull of shared identity: "we are the same kind of people". In the lunch scene it shows up as "developers like us" or "people from our part of town". It is the warmest principle and the hardest to see, because it feels like friendship rather than persuasion. Name it silently like the others.

You will also use these principles yourself, and you should, honestly. A second composite example. You are meeting a lender for a hypothetical construction loan. Authority, used honestly, is a report from a qualified cost consultant rather than your own estimate. Social proof, used honestly, is your record of delivering earlier projects on budget, with the evidence available. Commitment, used honestly, is asking the lender early what its credit committee needs to see, then delivering exactly that. Reciprocity, used honestly, is sending complete information before it is requested. The line you never cross is invented scarcity or authority: telling the lender another bank is ready to commit when it is not, or that an approval is certain when it is pending. That is no longer persuasion; it may be a misrepresentation, the subject of lesson 18, and lenders rarely forget it.

Before any important meeting, write three lines on a card: your walk-away number, the two facts you must verify, and the one thing you will not decide in the room. Read it before you go in and again before you answer any number.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is being moved by several principles at once, each harmless alone, until the price feels natural. The control is to name each principle silently as it appears, and to make no number decisions in the room that are not already on your signed paper.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner thinks the broker is being manipulative and becomes cold or rude. That costs him the relationship and teaches him nothing. These principles are how normal people persuade. Stay warm, stay curious, and stay on your numbers.

Callback

In lesson 6, Remi taught you to read every voice in a gate meeting with its incentive attached. Cialdini's principles are the methods those incentives use. The incentive tells you why someone is pushing; the principle tells you how; your signed numbers tell you whether it matters.

Recap

Cialdini's principles are reciprocity, commitment and consistency, social proof, authority, liking and scarcity, plus unity. Expect several in one meeting. Name them silently, verify claims, answer with your reasoning, and stay silent after their number. Build your own trust through reliability above all.

Next: Kema, Quiz and Recap — week 3, the psychology of deals.
checklist: Bring your signed walk-away price to every negotiation.
Name each influence principle silently as it appears.
Verify every second-hand authority claim directly with the source.
Answer questions about your budget with reasoning, not with your ceiling.
Stay silent after the other side names a number.
Make no price decision in the room that is not already on your paper.
Keep every promise of timing exactly, to build reliability.
head: Field checklist
speak: Across the table, people use a handful of influence principles that Robert Cialdini described: reciprocity, commitment and consistency, social proof, authority, liking and scarcity, and later unity. In one lunch with a seller's broker I might meet all six: he pays, he collects a small yes and then builds on it, he names other buyers, he quotes the planning director second-hand, we find we have a lot in common, and there is a Friday deadline. None of that changes my residual land value. So I name each principle silently, verify the authority claim myself, answer budget questions with reasoning rather than my ceiling, and stay silent after their number. I never say I really want this site. And I build my own trust through reliability: I send what I promised, when I promised it, and I give bad news early. That is how good deals reach me first.
terms: Influence principles — Cialdini's reciprocity, commitment and consistency, social proof, authority, liking and scarcity, later joined by unity.
Commitment and consistency — the pressure to act in line with something you have already agreed to or said.
Trust equation — Maister's practitioner model: credibility, reliability and intimacy raise trust; self-orientation lowers it.

hostile.q: From the seller's broker: I gave you this site before anyone else. I expected you to make it worth the seller's while. Is two point three really your answer?
hostile.a: I appreciate that you brought it to us first, and I will treat this as the priority it is. Two point three is what the building can carry at the return our lenders require. If the seller has information that changes our numbers, I will look at it before Friday.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 3 quiz and recap: the psychology of deals
summary: Six questions test the week: incentives and fee basis, Champlain Towers South and loss aversion, anchoring and residual land value, misrepresentation and the entire-agreement clause, sunk cost in the forward view, and Cialdini's principles and trust. A Red Pen drill and a boardroom drill put them to work.
body:
This week you learned why deals go wrong even when the numbers are known: incentives pull honest people, a certain loss feels larger than a probable one, the first number anchors, words in a meeting may not survive a contract, money spent pleads to be rescued, and pleasant pressure works. Today you produce it from memory.

Recall

Q. In lesson 17, what is the residual land value?

A. The most you can pay for land: completed value minus all non-land costs minus your required profit.

Q. In lesson 7, what four public gates does a project pass through?

A. Land use, building permit, inspections and occupancy.

Q. In lesson 18, what is a reliance list?

A. A written list of every fact you rely on before signing, each one verified independently or written into the contract.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the psychology of deals is invisible in a spreadsheet and decisive in a room. You will not remember a lesson in the moment the broker names a deadline. You will remember a habit. Answer aloud, then check, and mark the questions you hesitated on.

The six questions

Question 1. Your project manager is paid a monthly fee for as long as construction lasts. Which way does that pull, and how would you redesign it?

Answer: It pulls toward delay, because more months mean more fees. Cap the monthly fee at the planned duration and add a completion bonus for finishing by the reference-class date, reduced for each week late, with a lawyer drafting the terms.

Question 2. What decision pattern does Champlain Towers South illustrate, and what is Rule 3?

Answer: A certain, concentrated cost today weighed against an uncertain, invisible risk later, with the people who had to pay also controlling the timing; loss aversion pushed toward delay. Rule 3: when a qualified engineer reports a structural or life-safety defect, I fund and schedule the fix on the engineer's timeline. Cost, reassurance and the wish to wait never set the date.

Question 3. Completed value is $20 million, non-land costs are $14 million, and you require 15 percent profit on cost. What is your walk-away price for the land?

Answer: Maximum total cost is $20 million divided by 1.15, which is about $17,391,000. Subtract $14 million: the residual land value is about $3,391,000, including purchase costs.

Question 4. A broker tells you a site "has the best views in the city" and "is zoned for 50 units". Which matters legally, and what do you do about it?

Answer: The zoning claim is a statement of fact; the views claim is puffery. Verify the zoning with the authority having jurisdiction and, if you rely on it, write it into the contract as a representation or a condition, because an entire-agreement clause may stop you relying on what was only said.

Question 5. Why can a sunk cost never decide between two options?

Answer: Because it has already been spent in every option, so it subtracts out of the comparison. Compare options in the forward view, with the reference class applied to future costs and the opportunity cost of the capital stated.

Question 6. Name Cialdini's six original principles, and the one he added later.

Answer: Reciprocity, commitment and consistency, social proof, authority, liking and scarcity; he later added unity.

Say that out loud now.

Red Pen drill

Read this hypothetical note from a developer to his investors and find the defects.

We have agreed to buy the site for $2.8 million, a great result given the $3.2 million asking price. The broker confirmed it is zoned for 45 units, so we did not need a zoning condition; the contract has the seller's standard entire-agreement clause. Our architect, paid 7 percent of construction cost, recommends the premium facade package, which we have accepted. The building next door has an engineer's report recommending structural repairs; the owner says it can wait, so we have not looked into it. Two other developers were circling, so we had to move by Friday. We cannot walk away now because we have spent $350,000 on design.

The defects:

  1. "A great result given the asking price" measures the deal against the seller's anchor. There is no residual land value or walk-away price.
  2. Zoning relied on the broker's word, with no condition and an entire-agreement clause in the contract: a fact relied on but neither verified nor contracted.
  3. The facade recommendation came from someone paid a percentage of cost, accepted with no price and no evidence of added value.
  4. A neighbouring structural report was dismissed on reassurance from the person who would have to pay. It may affect your site, your construction and your neighbours; it needs a qualified engineer's view.
  5. "Two other developers were circling" is scarcity and social proof, unverified, used to justify speed.
  6. "We cannot walk away because we have spent $350,000" is sunk cost, rejected by Rule 1.

Boardroom drill

Two minutes, aloud, to an imaginary investment committee. Then compare.

"Deals rarely fail because the numbers were unknown; they fail because of how people behave around them. So I control the behaviour. Before I hire anyone I draw an incentive map and redesign fees that pull against me. Before I hear a seller's price I calculate the residual land value and sign a walk-away price, because the first number anchors everything after it. Every fact I rely on is verified or written into the contract, because an entire-agreement clause can make a broker's promise worthless. When a project goes sideways, I compare options from today forward and ignore money already spent. In negotiations I name the influence principles as they appear and stay on my paper. And when an engineer reports a life-safety defect, the engineer's timeline is the schedule: at Champlain Towers South, a repair debated for three years ended in a collapse that killed 98 people."

How to score yourself

One point per question answered aloud and correctly before reading the answer, and one per Red Pen defect found unaided, so twelve in total. Below nine, reread lessons 17 and 19, which hold the arithmetic. Then record the boardroom drill and listen once for three things: bottom line first, one number correct, and an ending on a rule.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is believing that knowing these biases protects you from them. It does not; research on biases generally finds that awareness alone is a weak defence. Procedures protect you: the signed walk-away price, the reliance list, the incentive map, the forward-view decision page.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner spots the biases in other people and never in himself. Turn every question this week on your own last decision: what anchored you, who was paid for what, and what did you rely on that was not written down?

A last practical step. Choose one procedure from this week and use it on a real decision in the next seven days, however small: draw an incentive map before you hire a trade, or write a walk-away price before you negotiate anything. A procedure used once becomes much easier to use when the stakes are high. Write down what it changed, if anything, and bring that note to next week's review. The goal is not a perfect week of decisions; it is one procedure that now runs without you having to remember it, which is the only kind that still works when someone is pressing you for an answer by Friday.

Callback

In lesson 8, Kema introduced the inside view and the outside view. Every bias this week is a way the inside view wins: the seller's anchor, the money already in, the pleasant broker, the reassuring owner. Every control this week is a way of bringing an outside number into the room and putting it on paper before the pressure arrives.

Recap

Incentives pull at the margin, so map and redesign them. Loss aversion favours delay and the status quo; Rule 3 puts life-safety on the engineer's timeline. Anchors are beaten by your own residual, set first. Facts you rely on must be verified or contracted. Sunk costs cancel; decide forward. Name the influence principles, and build trust through reliability.

terms: Anchoring — the pull of the first number on every later estimate.
Loss aversion — the tendency for a loss to feel roughly twice as painful as an equal gain feels good.
Residual land value — completed value minus all non-land costs minus required profit; the most the land can bear.

hostile.q: From an investor: you walked away from a site at two point eight when the asking was three point two. Were you not being too rigid?
hostile.a: No. Our residual land value was about $2.41 million, so at $2.8 million we would have overpaid by roughly $390,000 before construction began, measured against our own numbers rather than the seller's. Walking away from a deal that fails our arithmetic is the discipline you are paying me for.
